prize_parts.citation: for a poetry that has remade Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a sustained dialogue with inherited forms

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged but my citation is narrower. After the exchange I would credit the poetry alone, with the essays as a companion that is not named in the citation. Several colleagues, Sward, Olsson, Sem-Sandberg and Mattson among them, pressed the point that a citation covering both strands would lose focus and could pull the award toward critical and political writing. I agree. The claim I still find strongest is formal and linguistic: a decades-long poetic project, represented by Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses, that reopened the relation between Arabic poetry and its classical inheritance through myth and fragmentation without discarding that inheritance. On the common criteria, this is a distinctive voice, a formal and linguistic achievement that reaches a whole literary language, and an oeuvre long enough to be fully formed, so maturity here concerns the quality of the late work and not development. I do not prefer P000. Neither lead candidate is so imprecisely stated that no citation can be written, and the open questions are about verification, not about whether the writer is distinctive. I would not claim anything about sound or meter, since I cannot test it. Cărtărescu remains a very serious alternative. Under the chair's questions I weigh the asymmetry in what the committee can verify, and I explain below why that does not yet move me.
statement.case_against: The chair's question about evidence is the real weakness of my position. I cannot read Arabic prosody, and I cannot verify from the supplied evidence that the later collections sustain the quality of the landmark early books. My judgment rests on reception, public description and translation, which is thinner than what a colleague can bring to a prose candidate. I also accept the force of the point several colleagues made, that the Cărtărescu claim can be tested somewhat more directly through translated works. If the committee requires a claim it can partly verify, that argues for B012. Finally, my own earlier remarks about repetition in Cărtărescu are a reservation I could not substantiate, and I should not use them to discount him. The colleagues who raised the same worry called the recurrence of motifs a deliberate structure, and I cannot rule that out.

responses.point: Olsson treats translation risk as roughly symmetrical between the two lead candidates. He argues that Cărtărescu's architecture and imaginative scale are at least partly visible through translation, whereas the core of the Adonis claim is prosodic and intertextual work that none of us can test.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is the strongest argument against my preference. I do not think the risk is fully symmetrical. A claim about architecture can travel through translation better than a claim about prosody, so for the prose candidate the committee has more to work with. I concede that. I do not draw the conclusion that the unverifiable claim is the weaker one. The right response is a narrower citation that says only what the record supports, which is the renewal of poetic language through myth, fragmentation and dialogue with inherited forms. I would also test sufficiency. A poetic project that stays coherent across decades, in several translators' hands and in different forms, including the prose-poem and the long sequence, gives some indirect evidence that does not rest on the sound of the Arabic. That evidence is real but partial, and I do not call the question settled.

responses.point: Sward holds that translation risk bears harder on poetry than on prose, and that the shared reliance on a limited reception of poetry in translation should keep the citation modest. She also notes that unreadable achievement is not lesser achievement.
responses.response: I agree with her on the wording and with her caution about the two of us leaning on the same limited evidence. Her observation is correct that two members who prefer Adonis do not give independent confirmation, and I should not treat our agreement as evidence. I would push her slightly on one point. Saying that an unreadable achievement is not lesser is true, but it also does not make it established. The committee has to decide how much to rely on a claim it can verify only in part. My answer is to keep the citation on the poetry and on form, to leave out any claim about sound, and to state openly that the late collections are not covered by my knowledge. If colleagues who read Arabic or have followed the translations closely say that the later work lets the claim down, my case weakens a good deal.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argues that the formal control Cărtărescu shows over very large structures is a more fully legible achievement for a committee that cannot read the Arabic. He also asks that any citation be justified from specific works and not from reputation for scale.
responses.response: That test of justifying from specific works is one I apply to my own case too, and it is why I limit the Adonis citation to what the two named collections and the broader poetic project support. I accept that the Cărtărescu claim is more legible to us. I would still separate legibility from weight. His case seems to me to show that Blinding and Solenoid are controlled constructions. Whether the later work extends the method is a question he leaves open, and I cannot settle it either. On the Adonis side, I would be as strict about unverified claims as he is about Cărtărescu, which is why I would not claim more than formal renewal of poetic language in the citation.

responses.point: Mattson says she cannot resolve how much of the Adonis claim is the poems and how much is the essayistic and historical role, and that she would need colleagues who read Arabic to speak to this. She also moved Adonis up in her ordering after my case, though she would not prefer him.
responses.response: Her question about the split between poems and essays is the right one, and it is why I now propose a poetry-only citation. If the claim cannot be made for the poems, then it should not be made. I cannot supply the Arabic-language reading she asks for and I do not want to imply that I can. I would add that her position that she cannot prefer a candidate until the committee can say what survives translation is a coherent standard. By that standard my own preference is conditional. It stands on what I can state about voice and form, with the late work as the open test.

responses.point: Palm argues that the sustained architecture across several large works shows the sustained-quality criterion more clearly than she can establish for poetry through translation. She does not call the Adonis case weak.
responses.response: I accept that distinction and think it is fair to both candidates. Sustained quality is easier to show across several large prose works than across decades of poetry known through selected translations, and I cannot claim to have shown it for Adonis from the late collections. Where I differ is that I do not read this as a deficiency in the writer, since it is a limit of our access. That is why I keep B012 as my first alternative and not lower, and why I would not be reluctant if the committee preferred it after further discussion.

uncertainties: How much of the formal innovation in the Adonis poetry reaches readers in Swedish, English or French translation, and whether those translations are adequate witnesses for a committee that cannot read Arabic.
Whether the later collections sustain the quality of the early landmark books. My coverage of them is uneven and I cannot verify it.

Whether a poetry-only citation fairly represents an oeuvre in which the critical essays are a substantial body of work. I would keep them as a companion strand, but I am unsure how much that leaves out.
For Cărtărescu, whether recurring motifs across the large novels are development or elaboration of one mode. I cannot decide this and I do not use it as an argument against him.
Whether the asymmetry in what the committee can verify, which I accept is partly real, should count in favour of the more legible prose claim. I do not know how the committee should weigh it.
I have not independently read or verified any source and I rely on public knowledge, the shortlist descriptions and colleagues' round-1 statements.
Whether a co-opted member's vote reflects actual committee practice is undocumented, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no relationship with any shortlisted writer. My role as Permanent Secretary and my own non-fiction biography and journalism are context only and are not evidence of preference. My status as a co-opted member with undocumented voting rights is disclosed and not adjudicated. The disclosure by Sem-Sandberg of a thematic overlap with Magris is noted and does not bear on my preferred configuration.
